rationale: B wins because it guards the fact line instead of decorating around it. A tries to sell "Canva's AI acquisition is a bet that brand-safe image generation beats generic AI tools" and even says Canva "bought its way into proprietary AI capability," which is a bridge too far from the supplied facts. B catches the same temptation and refuses it: "The announcement does not connect them." That's the difference between a pitch strategist and a brochure machine.
gaps_in_A: "Canva's AI acquisition is a bet that brand-safe image generation beats generic AI tools" connects the acquisition to the enterprise AI feature without proof. The update gives both facts, not causation.

"Canva has converted just 24,000 of its 220 million users into paying teams" mixes users and teams as if they are comparable units. That ratio is interesting, but the wording overclaims the conversion math.
"Canva finally builds the SSO and admin controls IT departments were blocking it for" invents prior IT blockage. Plausible is not the same as reported.
"How a $26 billion private company keeps expanding without touching public markets" is usable, but it drifts toward IPO-market analysis without an IPO fact or capital-use evidence.
gaps_in_B: "220 million free users" is not in the update. The fact says monthly users; some may already be tied to paid teams.
"walks its 220 million users into Adobe and Microsoft's enterprise turf" is a little too neat. Consumer-scale reach is not the same as enterprise pipeline.
"who gets hurt" sharpens the competitive frame before there is customer, churn, pricing, or pipeline evidence. Good angle, but keep the knife in the drawer until proof arrives.

The refused "Canva adds SSO and admin tools" angle is too dismissive. As a bare feature item, yes, dull. As an IT procurement or security approval story with protocols and compliance proof, it could still work.
